title: Lesson 22: Building a Shared Team Playbook and Prompt Library
description: Turning private experiments into a common resource: one shared library with entries that carry real fields, a playbook of how the team uses AI, and owners and versions so the library does not rot.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building a Shared Team Playbook and Prompt Library", what is a team playbook as distinct from the prompt library?
options: The written agreement on how the team uses AI at all: tone, which tasks are handed to a tool, where data may go, and who checks what, while the library holds the working examples
A record of every prompt each person wrote privately
A tool that enforces permissions on AI usage
A report counting how many AI tasks the team ran
questions.explanation: The lesson says the playbook is the standards and the library is the working examples of those standards, and that together they turn private experiments into a common resource.

questions.question: Which fields does the lesson say a shared prompt entry needs to stay useful?
options: Only the prompt text with its placeholders
A name, a when-to-use line, the prompt with placeholders, a what-to-check note, and an example of the output
A name and the author's contact details
The model name and the cost per run
questions.explanation: The lesson says that without those fields a shared prompt is just an orphaned wall of text nobody trusts.

questions.question: Why does the lesson argue for versioning shared prompts?
options: So the library can be audited for compliance
So usage can be billed back to each team
Because one person tweaking a shared prompt for their own scenario can break it for everyone else, and without versions nobody can get the old one back
Because version numbers make the prompts run faster
questions.explanation: The lesson says versioning matters more the more people touch a shared prompt, and names the exact failure mode: a private tweak breaks the prompt for the rest of the team with no way to roll back.
